items.title: OpenAI partners with Google Cloud to offer frontier models and Codex workflows through Google Cloud Marketplace [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI models are coming to Google Cloud
items.summary:
OpenAI and Google Cloud have partnered to integrate OpenAI's frontier models and Codex agentic workflows into Google Cloud's Model Garden, enabling customers to access these models natively within Google Cloud's infrastructure. This integration supports complex AI workflows with Google's data governance and high-performance infrastructure, targeting enterprises including those in regulated industries.

The models will be available for purchase through the Google Cloud Marketplace, allowing enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments to apply those credits. OpenAI models will also be accessible via Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, providing customers with flexible model choices. General availability is planned in the coming weeks, expanding enterprise access to frontier AI models within Google Cloud's ecosystem.

items.originalTitle: OpenAI CLI
items.summary:
OpenAI has launched an official command-line interface (CLI) for its REST API, enabling users to interact with OpenAI services through a resource-based command structure. The CLI supports installation via Homebrew and Go, includes features like tab completion, update notifications, and detailed help commands, and requires API keys for standard and admin endpoints.

The tool offers commands for generating responses, managing files, and accessing administrative functions, with options for JSON output formatting and local file uploads. It also includes mechanisms to check for updates without automatic installation and supports multiple shell environments for command completion and shortcuts.

items.title: Developer fine-tunes a 360M-parameter language model to simulate a terminal interface by predicting screen changes from keypresses without a real shell or filesystem [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
items.summary:
A developer trained a 360 million parameter language model to act as a terminal by predicting how the screen changes in response to each keypress, without an underlying shell or filesystem. The model can create files, run programs like vim and tmux, play snake, and maintain short-term memory of commands. It was fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker containers.

The model treats the terminal as a grid of characters and outputs screen updates rather than text streams, using a small vocabulary of tokens to efficiently represent screen changes, including copying rows to handle scrolling. The demo runs in a browser with WebGPU support and is optimized for desktop use. This approach explores whether a language model can maintain a consistent interactive environment rather than just generating plausible terminal output.

items.title: OpenAI leads global coalition to coordinate response and patch critical PHP vulnerabilities discovered using GPT-5.6 Sol, emphasizing AI's dual role in security [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover vulnerabilities
items.summary:
OpenAI spearheaded a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source language widely used for websites and web applications. The flaws were identified using GPT-5.6 Sol as part of the Patch the Planet initiative, with contributions from partners like Wiz and Cloudflare. PHP maintainers led the fixes and releases, while OpenAI and collaborators coordinated research, technical support, and protections ahead of public disclosure.

The initiative included developing a PHP version checker to help organizations identify vulnerable versions and apply necessary updates. OpenAI highlighted the significance of these vulnerabilities due to PHP's widespread use and noted that frontier AI detected the flaws before attackers, creating a Defender’s Window for proactive mitigation. To support defenders with limited resources, OpenAI committed $1 billion in subsidized access to its Daybreak platform.

OpenAI also proposed a scalable framework for coordinated vulnerability response in the AI era, involving validation, fix development, advance notice to affected organizations, and collaboration with government agencies to protect critical infrastructure. This approach aims to streamline responses as AI capabilities uncover more security issues in widely used software.

items.title: OpenTelemetry enables detailed observability of AI agent workflows to trace execution paths, monitor costs, latency, and errors across multi-step LLM and tool calls [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Agent Observability with OpenTelemetry
items.summary:
AI agents orchestrate complex workflows involving multiple LLM calls and tool selections, making their execution paths difficult to trace and debug. OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral framework to capture telemetry data such as traces, metrics, and logs, enabling engineers to observe each step of an AI agent's run, including inputs, outputs, costs, and latencies.

This observability is crucial because AI agents can produce silent errors, non-deterministic outputs, and unpredictable costs due to dynamic tool usage and model calls. By instrumenting AI agents with OpenTelemetry and visualizing data through platforms like SigNoz Cloud, developers gain insights into agent behavior, helping them identify inefficiencies, debug issues, and optimize performance and cost.

items.title: Researchers propose Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation combining specialist merging and capability-guided supervision to improve student model training across six benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Policy Discrepancy: Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: Researchers introduce Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (CA-MOPD), a method that merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student model and adjusts supervision based on estimated capability gaps between teachers and the student. This approach addresses limitations of existing discrepancy-based supervision allocation by considering the student's current capabilities to modulate teacher guidance. CA-MOPD was evaluated on six benchmarks involving mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, achieving an average score of 32.22 and outperforming previous methods by up to 0.86 points. Controlled experiments confirm the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap-based supervision under matched training budgets.
items.description: Researchers introduce Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (CA-MOPD), a method that merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student model and adjusts supervision based on estimated capability gaps between teachers and the student. This approach addresses limitations of existing discrepancy-based supervision allocation by considering the student's current capabilities to modulate teacher guidance. CA-MOPD was evaluated on six benchmarks involving mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, achieving an average score of 32.22 and outperforming previous methods by up to 0.86 points. Controlled experiments confirm the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap-based supervision under matched training budgets.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.26950v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates domain specialists into a shared student, but determining how strongly each teacher should supervise remains challenging. Existing discrepancy-based allocation can assign strong supervision even when the student already matches or exceeds the teacher's task performance, since behavioral mismatch does not necessarily imply a remaining capability deficit. We propose Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (CA-MOPD), which combines specialist merging with capability-guided allocation to account for what the student has already learned. CA-MOPD first merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student initialization, then uses verifier-estimated teacher--student capability gaps to adjust domain-level distillation strength. Supervision decreases as capability gaps close and increases when estimated student capability regresses, while dense token-level guidance remains provided by the teachers. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, CA-MOPD achieves an average score of 32.22, outperforming naive MOPD, Open-MOPD, and the merged initialization by 0.86, 0.83, and 0.74 points, respectively. Controlled comparisons further support the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap guidance under matched training budgets.

items.title: CountVideoBench introduces a synthetic video benchmark to evaluate prediction biases in object counting by video-language models, revealing low accuracy and value-dependent biases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CountVideoBench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Prediction Biases on the Object Counting task by Video-Language Models
items.summary: CountVideoBench is a new benchmark comprising 2,600 synthetic videos with object counts ranging from 5 to 50, designed to assess counting capabilities of video-language models without confounding factors like object motion. The study evaluated sixteen models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting, finding no model exceeded 27.6% exact match accuracy and that models showed distinct biases toward certain preferred counts, with accuracy peaking at these values and dropping sharply at adjacent counts. These results highlight limitations in current models' counting abilities and the need for balanced benchmarks to better diagnose and improve this fundamental visual task.
items.description: CountVideoBench is a new benchmark comprising 2,600 synthetic videos with object counts ranging from 5 to 50, designed to assess counting capabilities of video-language models without confounding factors like object motion. The study evaluated sixteen models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting, finding no model exceeded 27.6% exact match accuracy and that models showed distinct biases toward certain preferred counts, with accuracy peaking at these values and dropping sharply at adjacent counts. These results highlight limitations in current models' counting abilities and the need for balanced benchmarks to better diagnose and improve this fundamental visual task.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.28356v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.

items.title: Researchers propose TURTLE, an unsupervised environment design method to evolve self-tuning benchmarks for long-horizon AI tool use, increasing task difficulty and diversity across multiple applications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use
items.summary:
Researchers introduce TURTLE (Tool Use Related Tasks with Long-Horizon Evolution), a method using large language model agents—a proposer, solver, and feedback generator—to evolve AI tool-use tasks without human supervision. TURTLE adapts test suites to various environments, supporting user simulators, document retrieval, and multi-app interactions, aiming to improve AI assistants' capabilities beyond simple chat interfaces.

Empirical evaluations on benchmarks like AppWorld, τ-Bench, and AutomationBench with the Gemma 4 31B-it model show that TURTLE increases the proportion of hard tasks by 165% on AppWorld, enhances task diversity in reasoning and tool interactions, and reveals a wider range of failure modes compared to original tasks. This approach addresses scalability and domain limitations of existing benchmarks for AI tool use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27307v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: For AI assistants to move beyond simple chat interfaces and reliably assist users with applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack, we need to improve their tool-use capabilities. However, existing tool use benchmarks are still limited and difficult to scale because they rely on human supervision or are too domain-specific. To make data generation scalable, we propose, TURTLE (Tool Use Related Tasks with Long-Horizon Evolution), an Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approach to evolve existing tasks using a proposer, a solver, and a feedback generator large language model agents. The proposer is rewarded for difficult yet solvable tasks based on the solver's empirical performance, and the feedback generator summarizes the solver's execution traces for the proposer to exploit. TURTLE produces evolving, self-tuning test suites adaptable to different environment requirements, from supporting user simulators and dense document retrieval to interacting across multiple apps. Empirical results on AppWorld, $\tau$-Bench, and AutomationBench using Gemma 4 31B-it show that the evolved tasks target the desired difficulty range (e.g., a 165% increase in the percentage of hard tasks on AppWorld), increase task diversity (in terms of reasoning and simultaneous tool interactions), and elicit a broader range of failure modes than the original tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce AuthorizationBench to evaluate LLM agents' adherence to user authorization, finding 19.2% of actions exceed granted permissions across 286 tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers developed AuthorizationBench, a benchmark to assess whether large language model (LLM) agents act within the authorization scope granted by users. Testing four models across 286 tasks in an authorization-aware sandbox, they found agents acted beyond their authorization in 19.2% of cases, with rates varying by configuration. The study highlights that task completion and reasoning effort do not guarantee authorization alignment, and agents consulting users before acting show lower rates of unauthorized behavior.

The benchmark includes tasks spanning various triggers, consequences, and application domains, producing 6,864 execution trajectories. Results indicate agents sometimes act out of authorization even without causing direct harm, and more often under benign pressures than malicious ones. This reveals a tension between agent autonomy and preserving user decision authority, suggesting the need for further human-centered research on authorization alignment in AI agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27548v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .

items.title: Researchers present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver for PDEs with constraints, enabling efficient forward and inverse problem solving across physics and engineering applications [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems
items.summary: Researchers have developed a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates constraints from large systems of equations arising in partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids. This solver supports linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, solves inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients and right-hand sides, and uses learnable graph coarsening to accelerate computations. The solver's stability and differentiability reduce the complexity of forward modeling and improve efficiency in related inverse problems, making it particularly useful for applications in geophysics where reducing model uncertainty is critical.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27888v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Approximate solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids can be represented on a graph. Numerical optimization involving stiff evolutionary and static PDEs often requires solving a large system of equations, which can be treated as a constraint. In this work, we present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint. We evaluate its performance across four key tasks: a) linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, b) solving inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients, c) solving inverse problems to estimate the right-hand side, and d) learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. The stability and differentiability of our solver enable significant reductions in the complexity of forward modeling while efficiently addressing related inverse problems. These capabilities make it a powerful tool for different physics and engineering applications, in particular for geophysics, where inverse problems are commonly solved in order to reduce the model uncertainty.

items.title: JetBrains Research presents Arend theorem prover based on homotopy type theory with cubical syntax and IntelliJ IDE integration
items.originalTitle: Theorem prover Arend
items.summary: JetBrains Research has developed Arend, a theorem prover designed to formalize mathematics within univalent foundations focusing on constructive mathematics. Arend uses a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax aligned with Martin-Löf Type Theory and features a flexible system of classes and records for constructing definition hierarchies. The Arend language is supported by an IntelliJ plugin that turns IntelliJ IDEA into a dedicated development environment, and its main library includes formalizations in constructive algebra, topology, and synthetic homotopy theory.
items.description: JetBrains Research has developed Arend, a theorem prover designed to formalize mathematics within univalent foundations focusing on constructive mathematics. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27264v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper is an exposition of the theorem prover Arend developed at JetBrains Research. Arend language has been designed to facilitate the formalization of mathematics within the framework of univalent foundations and with the focus on constructive mathematics. It is based on a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax that is more closely aligned with Martin-L\"of Type Theory (MLTT) than fully computational cubical type theories, while still retaining some of their computational properties useful in practice. Among the most notable features of the Arend language is its powerful system of classes and records supporting subsumptive subtyping, partial implementations and anonymous extensions, which provides extensive flexibility for constructing hierarchies of definitions. Formalization in Arend is streamlined by the IntelliJ Arend plugin, which transforms IntelliJ IDEA into a full-fledged integrated development environment (IDE) for the Arend language. The main Arend library arend-lib includes formalizations in constructive algebra, topology and synthetic homotopy theory.

items.title: Researchers introduce S2-MAS, a multi-agent simulation framework with 500 million synthetic household personas for society-scale economic modeling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with 500 Million Household Persona Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed S2-MAS, a society-scale multi-agent simulation framework that models economic responses using 500 million synthetic household personas based on real survey data. The framework features the Genese engine, which separates decision-making from state updates, and includes financial scenarios and ledgers to track consumption, cash, debt, and payments. A compact decision model trained on millions of examples outperforms previous models in consumer financial-choice tasks.

The team evaluated eight financial task families and simulated 12 million distinct household agents under various purchase and funding conditions, observing how changes in purchase goals and credit limits affect consumption across different demographic groups. The simulation captures differences in education, employment, household size, and financial behaviors such as cash drawdown and debt repayment. A 24-month panel study varied purchase goals under a common credit product, updating offers based on repayment and arrears.

S2-MAS links diverse household decisions to evolving financial outcomes, enabling economic experiments across household groups, population scales, and time horizons, supporting detailed analysis of consumption, cash flow, and repayment patterns in large populations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27746v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simulating economic responses at society scale requires agents whose decisions reflect household circumstances and the effects of earlier actions. We introduce S$^2$-MAS, a society-scale multi-agent simulation framework built on 500 million synthetic household personas grounded in real-survey data. Its Genese engine separates decisions from state updates, while reusable financial scenarios and application ledgers track consumption, cash, debt and payments. Sharp-421m-mlx, a compact decision model trained with SFT + RLCD on 2.93 million examples, achieves 74.55% accuracy and 38.37% question-macro F1 in consumer financial-choice scenarios, outperforming Jev 1.13 and GLM-5.3-Flash on both measures. We evaluate eight financial task families and simulate 12 million distinct household agents in paired purchase-funding conditions. Jointly raising purchase goals and approved credit limits increases consumption, with responses differing across age and income groups. Education, employment and household-size differences persist after age--income standardization and mainly reflect transitions from deferral to purchase. Asset and debt groups differ in cash drawdown, repayment and closing debt. A 24-month panel varies purchase goals under a common credit product, with repayment and arrears updating subsequent offers. S$^2$-MAS links heterogeneous household decisions to evolving consumption, cash and repayment paths, supporting economic experiments across household groups, population scales and time horizons.

items.title: RayCo4D introduces a ray-conditioned continuous motion model for monocular 4D dynamic scene reconstruction, improving novel-view synthesis and temporal consistency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RayCo4D: Ray-Conditioned Continuous Motion Model for Monocular 4D Dynamic Reconstruction
items.summary: RayCo4D presents a new approach for reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video by separating visual measurements from latent 3D motion states and associating each track with a reference-time 3D query constrained to its camera ray. The model uses shared latent motion nodes with SE(3) poses and velocities, coupled by a white-noise-on-acceleration prior to enable continuous-time interpolation and joint constraint of latent states across visibility intervals. Experiments demonstrate that RayCo4D achieves competitive novel-view synthesis quality, enhances structural and temporal consistency during rapid motion and incomplete tracks, and supports continuous-time rendering for diverse monocular dynamic scenes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.28351v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video requires inferring motion from noisy and intermittently visible observations. Long-range tracks provide valuable geometric constraints, but integrating their fragmented temporal coverage into shared, continuous motion remains challenging. We introduce RayCo4D, a ray-conditioned continuous motion model for monocular 4D reconstruction that explicitly separates visual measurements from latent 3D motion states. Each track is associated with a reference-time 3D query constrained to its camera ray, and its image and depth observations constrain shared latent motion nodes through local many-to-many associations. Each node maintains an $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ pose and body-frame velocity at sparse support times. A white-noise-on-acceleration process prior couples neighboring states and defines continuous-time interpolation, allowing observations across visibility intervals to jointly constrain the same latent state sequence. The inferred shared motion is transferred to Gaussian primitives through dual-quaternion blending, while reference-anchored local $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ residuals capture fine-scale non-rigid deformation beyond the shared scaffold. Experiments on diverse monocular dynamic scenes show that RayCo4D achieves competitive novel-view synthesis quality, improves structural and temporal consistency under rapid motion and incomplete tracks, and supports continuous-time rendering.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.16975v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

items.title: Researchers introduce VLA-Rolling, an adaptive inference framework that reuses action tails to reduce denoising steps and improve control in vision-language-action models across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: VLA-Rolling: Fewer Denoising Steps, Better Control via Adaptive Action Reuse
items.summary:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically discard unexecuted action tails during iterative denoising, but researchers show these tails retain useful denoising progress that can be reused to improve efficiency and accuracy. They propose VLA-Rolling, a lightweight framework that inherits action tails, estimates confidence per action, and refines actions through adaptive renoising and denoising budget allocation without retraining the underlying model.

VLA-Rolling was tested on several VLA models including π0.5, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 across benchmarks such as LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0. It reduced inference costs in all 16 model-benchmark pairs with up to 1.48× speedup and improved success rates in 14 pairs by up to 15.08 percentage points. These results demonstrate that action tails are reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference with fewer denoising steps.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.25043v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.

items.title: Researchers formulate Heisenberg antiferromagnet Hamiltonians and ground-state sign structures using graph theory, linking them to weighted Max-Cut problems on Hilbert graphs
items.originalTitle: Graph-Theoretic Formulation of Hamiltonian and Ground-State Sign Structures in Heisenberg Antiferromagnets
items.summary:
Researchers present a graph-theoretic approach to studying Heisenberg antiferromagnets by representing their Hamiltonians as weighted Laplacians of Hilbert graphs, where vertices correspond to spin configurations and edges connect configurations differing by spin exchanges. This framework relates the exact ground-state energy to the largest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian and connects phase optimization to classical antiferromagnetic models and weighted Max-Cut problems on these graphs.

The study shows that when the Hilbert graph is bipartite, a diagonal sign transformation removes positive off-diagonal Hamiltonian elements, reproducing the Marshall sign rule via graph two-coloring; otherwise, the minimal positive weight corresponds to edges uncut by Max-Cut. This unified graph formulation provides insights into wave function sign structures, Hamiltonian stoquasticity, and challenges in variational and quantum Monte Carlo methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.04943v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study Heisenberg antiferromagnets through a graph-theoretic representation of their Hamiltonians. In the computational basis of a fixed-magnetization sector, the Heisenberg Hamiltonian equals a constant minus the weighted Laplacian of a graph whose vertices are spin configurations and whose edges connect configurations related by exchanging two antiparallel spins on a lattice bond. We call this graph the Hilbert graph (HG) which is isomorphic to the token graph of the lattice over which the Hamiltonian is defined. The exact ground-state energy is then determined by the largest eigenvalue of the HG Laplacian, which is the spectral relaxation of weighted Max-Cut on the HG. With the amplitudes fixed, the phase-dependent part of the variational energy defines an antiferromagnetic classical XY model on the HG, with couplings set by the amplitudes. Restricting the variational state to be real, i.e., restricting its phases to $\{0,\pi\}$, reduces the fixed-amplitude energy minimization to solving an antiferromagnetic Ising model and hence a weighted Max-Cut on the HG. When the weights are generated from non-degenerate ground-state amplitudes, the optimal phases give the ground-state sign structure which can be recovered from the weights in time polynomial in the size of the HG. On the Hamiltonian side, a diagonal sign transformation removes all positive off-diagonal matrix elements if and only if the HG is bipartite, which reproduces the Marshall sign rule on bipartite lattices through the graph two-coloring problem; otherwise, the minimal remaining positive weight equals the sum of HG edge weights left uncut by the Max-Cut. This graph formulation establishes a common framework for understanding wave function sign structure, Hamiltonian stoquasticity, non-convexity of phase optimization in variational Monte Carlo, and the average sign in quantum Monte Carlo.

items.title: WeGR introduces behavior-aware tokenization and preference alignment to improve generative retrieval in industrial search, achieving gains in orders, CTR, and CVR with reduced resource usage [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WeGR: Towards Unified Generative Retrieval via Behavior-aware Tokenization and Preference Alignment
items.summary: WeGR is a unified generative retrieval framework designed to enhance industrial search by incorporating user behavior signals through a novel tokenizer and preference alignment method. It addresses challenges in preserving collaborative signals and sparse reward issues in reinforcement learning by using a Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (CoCo-VAE) and Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO). Extensive offline tests show improved retrieval and ranking, while a six-week online A/B test on a large e-commerce platform demonstrated increases of 2.539% in orders, 1.508% in click-through rate, and 1.381% in conversion rate, alongside reductions in CPU and GPU usage by over 25%. These results indicate WeGR's effectiveness and efficiency in real-world deployment, supporting multiple search scenarios with high traffic.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.16979v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) offers a promising paradigm for industrial search by unifying candidate generation within an autoregressive framework. However, effectively leveraging user behaviors in industrial GR remains challenging: existing SID tokenization methods struggle to preserve collaborative signals while maintaining balanced codebook utilization, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) for prioritizing high-value candidates suffers from sparse rewards when generated SIDs fail to match positive items. To address these challenges, we propose WeGR, a unified GR framework with two complementary components. Specifically, the Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (CoCo-VAE) injects query-to-item and item-to-item collaborative signals into continuous representations before quantization, preserving behavioral information without disrupting codebook optimization. It further couples first-layer codebook refresh to reactivate underutilized codewords with fidelity anti-collapse regularization, which broadens gradient coverage over relevant codewords and penalizes collisions in deeper layers to yield behavior-aware SIDs with balanced utilization. For preference alignment, Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO) progressively expands reward evaluation and policy optimization horizons to alleviate reward sparsity, enabling coarse-to-fine preference learning from SID prefixes to complete items without auxiliary reward models. Extensive offline experiments validate that WeGR improves retrieval and ranking performance. Moreover, a six-week online A/B test on a large-scale e-commerce search platform achieves relative gains of 2.539% in orders, 1.508% in CTR, and 1.381% in CVR, while reducing CPU and GPU usage by 25.5% and 26.1%. These results highlight the effectiveness and efficiency of WeGR in industrial deployment, supporting multiple search scenarios and tens of millions of daily page views.

items.title: SkillEval framework uses cognitive diagnosis models to generate interpretable skill profiles for 3,811 LLMs across five benchmarks, improving evaluation granularity and prediction of model behavior [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillEval: Learning Interpretable Ability Profiles of LLMs via Cognitive Diagnosis Models
items.summary:
SkillEval introduces a new evaluation framework that moves beyond single scalar scores by analyzing large language models (LLMs) at the skill level using cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs). It leverages LLMs' meta-cognitive abilities to identify interpretable skills from benchmark questions and estimates per-skill abilities, providing more calibrated and informative model profiles than traditional average-based methods. The study evaluated 3,811 LLMs on 9,523 items across five diverse benchmarks including MATH and BBH.

The framework demonstrates practical benefits in two downstream tasks: dynamically routing queries to the most capable yet efficient model, reducing inference costs by over 60% while improving performance, and enabling efficient evaluation of unseen models through Computerized Adaptive Testing. Additionally, SkillEval's skill profiles offer insights into skill sharing across benchmarks and differences between instruction-tuned and base models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.28767v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.

items.title: Researchers develop an in-house System 1 judge using LoRA adapters to triage coding sessions at 1% of frontier LLM cost and evaluate open LoRA models on JevBench with competitive accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Our Own Jev: Typed Decisions in One Forward Pass, from an In-House Judge to Open LoRA Models
items.summary:
Researchers present a typed decision approach that computes probabilities for fixed options in one forward pass by reading language model logits or a small head over hidden states, avoiding text generation and parsing. They describe an in-house System 1 judge that triages about 148,000 coding session records, replacing a costly frontier LLM judge with a self-hosted frozen backbone and LoRA adapter, reducing cost to roughly 1% and processing 1,000 sessions in about three minutes on one GPU.

The study also evaluates whether a readout adding no parameters can be competitive by applying the Eikos recipe and a corpus of 25,000 decisions to three LoRA-adapted decoder backbones (1B, 2B, and 35B parameters). Their 35B model scores 79.3% on 111 hard JevBench items, comparable to a commercial reference at 73.0%, and outperforms several open systems. They find no benefit from training the output layer's letter rows, and retraining on a later corpus release improves the 2B model's accuracy by 11.7 points, highlighting the limitations of small evaluations.

items.title: OmniSimulator trains small language models with structured behavior-oriented reasoning to improve realistic user simulation on short-video platforms [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OmniSimulator: Aligning Small Language Models for Authentic Heterogeneous Behavior Modeling
items.summary: Researchers propose OmniSimulator, a training framework that enhances small language models' ability to simulate authentic user behavior by organizing reasoning into a five-dimensional schema and using high-quality data from real user interactions. The approach employs a teacher model to generate detailed reasoning traces, helping smaller models learn meaningful behavior patterns rather than superficial correlations. Using nearly 10,000 training instances from three months of data on 200 users, OmniSimulator improved the Qwen3-8B model's performance by over 34%, achieving results comparable to larger models like Claude-Sonnet-4.5 while enabling smaller-scale, self-hosted deployment. These findings suggest that structured behavior-oriented reasoning can enable scalable, high-fidelity user simulation with smaller language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.29472v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential as general-purpose user simulators for interactive systems. Prior studies have demonstrated that training on high-quality data can substantially improve model reasoning and downstream task performance. However, the upper bound of user simulation is still constrained by the model's reasoning paradigm: native chain-of-thought often degenerates into shallow pattern matching and fails to adequately model the behavioral factors underlying real user decisions. In this paper, we propose OmniSimulator, a novel training framework designed to improve the predictive ability of small LLMs for realistic user simulation on short-video platform environments. Specifically, OmniSimulator organizes behavior-oriented reasoning through a structured schema with five dimensions, carefully selects data from real user-behavior scenarios, and introduces a teacher model to generate high-quality reasoning traces under the proposed schema, helping small models learn behavior-relevant reasoning patterns rather than relying on superficial behavioral correlations. Based on this process, we construct 9,881 high-quality training instances from three months of historical interaction trajectories of 200 real users, averaging about 50 distilled examples per user. Experimental results show that OmniSimulator improves the average score of Qwen3-8B by 34.33%, achieves performance competitive with Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and supports smaller-scale, self-hosted deployment. These results suggest that learning structured behavior-oriented reasoning patterns is a promising direction towards scalable and high-fidelity LLM-based user simulation.

items.title: Mitigating Query Shortcuts in Chain-of-Thought with Context-Aware Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mitigating Query Shortcuts in Chain-of-Thought with Context-Aware Decoding
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29518v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have shown that final answers do not always depend on the generated rationales. In particular, LLMs may rely on query-specific shortcuts rather than the information provided by their reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate whether context-aware decoding (CAD), an existing contrastive decoding method, can mitigate such shortcut behavior when applied to CoT reasoning. We study this application as Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD), which contrasts the next-token distributions conditioned on the query with and without its rationale, amplifying tokens whose likelihood increases due to the rationale. We provide a theoretical interpretation of this decoding rule via a KL-regularized reward-maximization objective. Experiments across five reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RCD improves answer accuracy over standard CoT. Furthermore, intervention analyses using ground-truth and random rationales reveal that RCD increases the behavioral dependence of final answers on the rationale content. Our findings suggest that contrastive decoding offers a simple, training-free approach to mitigating query shortcuts.

items.title: Where Do LLMs Learn to Recommend AI? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Do LLMs Learn to Recommend AI?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29785v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Asked what to study, which career to pursue, or what product to build, large language models (LLMs) often recommend AI-related options. We ask where this tendency comes from by comparing models before and after fine-tuning and by varying how questions are asked. First, pretrained models already include explicit AI/ML terms in the recommendations of 27% of their responses, and their released instruction-tuned versions do so in 59%. Second, fine-tuning models ourselves shows that this rise is not inevitable: general instruction tuning leaves the rate unchanged, but removing the 7% of instruction examples that concern AI cuts it by 14 percentage points, below the level of the pretrained models it starts from. Data rewarding helpfulness raise it by 9 points, while data ranked by the preferences of diverse simulated users lower it by 9. Finally, with models held fixed, asking for the "best" option or for what to do "right now" raises the rate by 8 and 18 points, whereas telling the model it is an AI advisor adds 4. Overall, the tendency starts in pretraining, and what models learn afterward, together with how a question is phrased, decides how strongly it appears.

items.title: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29922v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline.

items.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.28763v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

items.originalTitle: CALLIOPE: Private Insights into AI Use, Without Embeddings
items.summary: arXiv:2610.28797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce CALLIOPE, a top-down framework for discovering topic hierarchies in large corpora of unstructured data (e.g., LLM conversations), while supporting differential privacy (DP). items.title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise
items.summary: arXiv:2610.28810v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.

items.title: TeachBack: Learning to Teach via Bidirectional Preference Optimization for On-Policy Self-Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TeachBack: Learning to Teach via Bidirectional Preference Optimization for On-Policy Self-Distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29167v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables a language model to learn from a Teacher instantiated from the same model but given access to privileged information, such as a reference solution. We find that access to sufficient privileged information allows the Teacher to generate highly accurate trajectories; however, accuracy alone does not guarantee that these trajectories are suitable for Student learning. Direct access to a complete solution may encourage shortened, reference-conditioned derivations that omit the exploration, verification, and self-correction required to solve problems without privileged information. We introduce TeachBack, a bidirectional preference-learning framework for on-policy self-distillation that learns not only from the Teacher but also how the Teacher should teach. TeachBack shapes the Teacher's generation behavior by controlling the length of the reference-reasoning suffix injected into the prompt and by varying the prompt style. While maintaining comparable Teacher accuracy, it encourages the Teacher to explore and re-solve problems, thereby reducing its reliance on the reference solution. At each rollout refresh, the shared policy generates both a privileged Teacher trajectory and a problem-only Student trajectory. A pairwise preference objective uses privileged Teacher trajectories to improve Student learning, while the reversed preference uses the Student's behavior to shape future Teacher supervision under the privileged condition. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show that TeachBack consistently improves Student performance over existing OPSD methods and related baselines.

items.title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent harnesses have become a central component of modern agentic systems, shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing approaches typically train through a single fixed harness, which can lead to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Harness Scaling}, a new scaling dimension for agentic RL that extends training from a single harness to diverse execution configurations. Concretely, we construct a factorized harness space, select a compact training subset with balanced factorial coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage with controlled variation for the same task. Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations. Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models trained through a single complex black-box harness. These results establish harness diversity as a meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for cross-harness generalization.

items.title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29812v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.

items.title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

items.title: Agent Behavior Maps: Locating Agents by What They Would Do, Without Running Them [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agent Behavior Maps: Locating Agents by What They Would Do, Without Running Them
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. An Agent Behavior Map represents LLM-harness combinations using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, without requiring new environment rollouts from the target agent. We derive error bounds relating squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL under explicit assumptions, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track the directly measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. In ALFWorld, these similarities persist after controlling for success rates and model size, including across model families. As an extension, harness-component displacements approximately compose, with accuracy varying across components and environments.

items.title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30128v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user's interaction history, regardless of the item's contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non-uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non-uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already-converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality. These observations motivate a shift from fixed-depth computation to item-level adaptive reasoning. To this end, we propose LoopRec. LoopRec recursively applies a single weight-shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit-or-continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. This design converts the fixed global depth into a learned, per-item property without auxiliary depth labels, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks with four backbone families demonstrate that LoopRec consistently outperforms matched fixed-depth counterparts. Further analysis reveals that LoopRec's learned allocation exhibits interpretable patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: lower-frequency items and more recent interactions naturally receive deeper computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Elpmis117/LoopRec.

items.title: Hyperdimensional Probe: Decoding LLM Representations via Vector Symbolic Architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Hyperdimensional Probe: Decoding LLM Representations via Vector Symbolic Architectures
items.summary: arXiv:2509.25045v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite their capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain opaque with limited understanding of their internal representations. Current interpretability methods either focus on input-oriented feature extraction, such as supervised probes and Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), or on output distribution inspection, such as logit-oriented approaches. A full understanding of LLM vector spaces, however, requires integrating both perspectives, something existing approaches struggle with due to constraints on latent feature definitions. We introduce the Hyperdimensional Probe, a hybrid supervised probe that combines symbolic representations with neural probing. Leveraging Vector Symbolic Architectures (VSAs) and hypervector algebra, it unifies prior methods: the top-down interpretability of supervised probes, SAE's sparsity-driven proxy space, and output-oriented logit investigation. By combining the supervised learning paradigm of traditional probes with the dictionary-based representation principle of SAEs, our approach enables deeper input-focused feature extraction while supporting output-oriented analysis. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently extracts meaningful semantic information across different LLMs, embedding sizes, and configurations, uncovering concept-oriented insights into LLM inference across two distinct scenarios: input-completion tasks and QA-focused text generation. VSA-based probing overcomes the limitations of logit-based analyses, which are constrained by the model's token vocabulary, while also mitigating the noisier interpretability outcomes often produced by SAEs in settings with a bounded conceptual feature space. By supporting a joint investigation of input-output features, this work advances the semantic understanding of neural representations while unifying the complementary perspectives of prior methods.

items.title: The Stepwise Informativeness Assumption: When Do Entropy Dynamics Track Reasoning Correctness in LLMs? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Stepwise Informativeness Assumption: When Do Entropy Dynamics Track Reasoning Correctness in LLMs?
items.summary: arXiv:2604.06192v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work uses entropy-based signals at multiple representation levels to study reasoning in large language models, but the field remains largely empirical. From a theoretical perspective, reductions in model uncertainty do not necessarily reflect progress toward correctness. In this work, we characterize when such alignment can be expected through the Stepwise Informativeness Assumption (SIA), which requires entropy-reducing reasoning-prefix extensions increase the probability assigned to valid answers in expectation. We show that next-token prediction can transfer answer-relevant information from training data to the model, but does not, by itself, guarantee alignment with correctness. Instead, we propose that this alignment depends on how the training regime couples reasoning traces to correct answers. Furthermore, we hypothesize observable signatures of this phenomenon and characterize its expected failure regimes. We empirically investigate how entropy dynamics relate to correctness across four reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, ARC, SVAMP, MATH) and diverse open-weight language models spanning base, instruction-tuned, and RL-trained regimes. Our results show that entropy-correctness alignment strengthens with post-training but can weaken when task difficulty exceeds model capabilities.

items.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21561v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

items.summary: arXiv:2601.13235v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Caregivers seeking AI-mediated support express complex needs---information-seeking, emotional validation, and distress cues---that warrant careful evaluation of response safety and appropriateness. Existing AI evaluation frameworks, primarily focused on general risks (toxicity, hallucinations, policy violations, etc), may not adequately capture the nuanced risks of LLM-responses in caregiving-contexts. We introduce RubRIX (Rubric-based Risk Index), a theory-driven, clinician-validated framework for evaluating risks in LLM caregiving responses. Grounded in the Elements of an Ethic of Care, RubRIX operationalizes five empirically-derived risk dimensions: Inattention, Bias & Stigma, Information Inaccuracy, Uncritical Affirmation, and Epistemic Arrogance. We evaluate six state-of-the-art LLMs on over 20,000 caregiver queries from Reddit and ALZConnected. Rubric-guided refinement consistently reduced risk-components by 45-98% after one iteration across models. This work contributes a methodological approach for developing domain-sensitive, user-centered evaluation frameworks for high-burden contexts. Our findings highlight the importance of domain-sensitive, interactional risk evaluation for the responsible deployment of LLMs in caregiving support contexts. We release benchmark datasets to enable future research on contextual risk evaluation in AI-mediated support.

items.title: Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory
items.summary: arXiv:2602.18297v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors are LLM-based systems that analyze reasoning traces to detect when outputs may exhibit attributes of interest, such as test-hacking behavior during code generation. In this paper, we use information-theoretic analysis to show that non-zero mutual information between CoT and output is a necessary but not sufficient condition for CoT monitorability. We identify two sources of approximation error that may undermine the performance of CoT monitors in practice: information gap, which measures the extent to which the monitor can extract the information available in CoT, and elicitation error, which measures the extent to which the monitor approximates the optimal monitoring function. Empirically, we show that CoT obfuscation can arise even in the absence of any optimization pressure against CoT. We further demonstrate that the fragility of CoT monitorability can be systematically mitigated through targeted training objectives. To this end, we propose a practical, label-free objective based on mutual information between outputs and CoTs, and benchmark it against an oracle-based method that directly rewards the monitored model for CoTs that maximize monitor accuracy. Across multiple environments, we show that our objective is effective at preventing CoT obfuscation even when training against a monitor, and helps mitigate reward hacking when the task reward is imperfectly specified.

items.title: Rethinking Synthetic Rationale Supervision for Disease Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rethinking Synthetic Rationale Supervision for Disease Prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2606.10279v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning with synthetic rationales is widely assumed to improve clinical prediction by teaching models not only what to predict but why. We test this assumption on five-year Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) prediction from longitudinal health histories. In this setting, we generate training rationales using the correct labels, then fine-tune models to output a rationale followed by a label. Across a large-scale controlled experiment of 504 configurations, we find that Rationale First SFT consistently and substantially hurts predictive performance relative to Label Only fine-tuning. The degradation persists across model families and data scales, and is not resolved by using a reasoning-oriented base model. A fixed-protocol cardiovascular disease (CVD) validation reproduces similar findings. Crucially, the failure is not explained by poor rationale quality: human expert annotation confirms that the generated rationales are medically accurate and faithfully grounded in patient-specific evidence, and few-shot experiments show that the same rationales improve performance when used as inference-time demonstrations rather than training targets. A simple label-ordering intervention clarifies the mechanism: placing the prediction before the same rationale restores predictive performance. This suggests that conditioning predictions on generated rationales contributes to the degradation. We hope our work paves the way toward a more precise understanding of when and how rationale-based supervision helps and when it does not, guiding the responsible development of language models for high-stakes clinical prediction.

items.title: DFAH-Bench: What Agreement Leaves Unmeasured in Financial Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DFAH-Bench: What Agreement Leaves Unmeasured in Financial Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2607.20491v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a financial agent repeats its decision, how much does that tell us about the actions behind it? DFAH-Bench examines this question through replay experiments, a controlled test of omitted tool calls, and banking tasks with authorization checks. Across 570 eligible prospective replay episodes, decisions agreed at rates of 94-95%, while tool paths, including inputs and results, agreed at 45-52%; one condition fell one group short of the planned minimum. In a separate 48-execution diagnostic, deleting the same calls from repeated records left agreement perfect. In banking probes, repeated authorization decisions sometimes conflicted with constructed rule labels. The $\tau$-Knowledge banking study scheduled 1,080 episodes, with 1,033 known outcomes. Structural checks alone completed more primary tasks than either model-based gate-and-recovery bundle. Input limits and recovery behavior materially shape these results. The typed-choice bundle had lower mean episode cost than the generative bundle on complete task pairs, but fewer successes across the primary schedule under every assignment of unknown outcomes. Missing outcomes prevented the planned confirmatory tests, so the banking comparisons are descriptive. Together, the findings show that agreement alone cannot establish reliability: it can conceal changes in execution, systematic omissions, and unsupported decisions. Evaluation therefore needs to connect what the agent did, the evidence and rules governing its action, and whether it completed the task.
